.
FYI

The English word Senate comes from the Latin SENATUS which in turn derives from the Latin SENEX which it means “old man” or “elderly.” And therefore, SENATUS (Latin) or Senate (English) means “assembly of the elderly.”

Got the idea?
.

"Jason Koebler noted that Americans are sick of being told they should “shut up and suffer” while tech barons make scads of money and economically and spiritually impoverish the rest of us by automating our jobs and humanity away. His term for the corrupt status quo is “the depravity economy."

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/americas-new-no-employee-small-business-owners-start-hot-in-ai-era.html
https://www.ft.com/content/47dba9d2-4c82-4e17-969d-f1728ef13a5a?syn-25a6b1a6=1

Is the argument that there is mass impoverishment or is the argument that tech barons making a scad of money? Those are non-equivalent. Would Ms. Grose prefer, for instance, a pre-Industrial Revolution society? 

As for the spiritual aspects--do armchair thinkers really prioritize them over the jobs created, the medical treatments innovated and the hope generated by AI? If you don't believe that  is happening, see: https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20260309-ai-is-finding-treatments-for-incurable-diseases

She was genuinely afraid.  Mostly afraid of falling and breaking a hip, as she had seen so many do, to the point where after a fall that did not break a hip, she would not get up and do PT with most therapist, afraid she would fall.  She had constant back pain from cracked vertebrae.  She was always kind, but the anxiety impaired her as much as her physical limitations.  A mild anti anxiety pill prescribed by her doctor, and then by hospice (which over 18 months) gave her more quality of life in the end.

comments.name: P. Drake
comments.body:
According to LW, LW's mother is a complainer.  And that, for LW, is the problem.  The problem is a global one.  LW doesn't seem to be interested in whether one or more of the things the mother complains about are actually things to be concerned about or justify the complaints.  She just, according to LW, complains about everything.

Quite plausibly, the mother overdoes it, as LW says.  But I don't see a very fine-grained view on LW's part of what those things are that she complains about, or much curiosity.  The problem for LW seems to be one of "trying to end calls with her," but is she right about anything?  There is no indication here that LW takes mother seriously as a rational person.  Maybe it would help to prioritize things and concentrate on what is most important.  LW says that the facility offers "extensive services," but does that mean that mother's complaints are groundless and should be dismissed?  Or redirected to a bot?  At least when you call Customer Service, when you say "agent," you can still sometimes get a live person!

comments.name: BB
comments.body: I had a mother, she in FL, me in NJ, that was similar to that of the LW.  From experience as a Dir of Marketing in senior housing, and certificate in gerontology, please be advised that your mother will NOT change so it's time to stop trying to because she is not looking for advice from you.  She has the psychiatrist for that. Just listen, say "uh huh", "oh, that's too bad", "ok, mom I have work to do, dinner is ready, etc., I'll talk to you tomorrow."  It may take some getting used to on your part but well worth it.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
Many commenters clearly ignored the line "we could offer her a clearly identified chatbot" - it would be her choice to turn on the computer or pick up the phone and call one of her children. The letter writer is exhausted because they care and want to be there for her.

Social engagement helps to hold off, and can even reverse, mental decline. Using a chatbot, which involves language understanding and construction, may offer some fraction of that. Far better than just ignoring her calls or telling her "you're an emotional vampire, stop feeding off us".

The writer also already uses AI, social ills aside - arguments against AI are going to fall on deaf ears.

comments.name: Here There And Everywhere
comments.body:
I realized in my situation that mother was never happy unless she had something to be unhappy about. That was who she was. There was no ever making her happy. She enjoyed being miserable. 

The LW needs to realize this is who his mother is. She is never going to change. The only thing that can change is his response to the situation.  Just get off the phon --hang up if you have to--e or get up and leave a visit when she starts in. Limit the amount of time for your visits and how often you visit,.

It is soul sucking to be around someone like this.

comments.name: faye
comments.body: Why on earth is the letter writer or her brother putting up with their mother's behavior? Why are they being such doormats? End the phone call/leave the room whenever mom complains/is negative. By continuing to engage, you are reinforcing/rewarding mom's bad behavior. If you detach/end the call when mom complains, she'll eventually learn that she can't do that if she wants to retain your attention. It won't be easy -- you've indulged her bad behavior for decades. But it's not too late to establish boundaries: what behavior/treatment do you want to accept? What do you not? Seems that the letter writer and her brother would benefit from some self-worth counseling

comments.name: Mythical
comments.body: “She takes medication prescribed by a psychiatrist and attends regular counseling,” so she must have some awareness of her issues and doesn’t always “refuse to admit she needs help.”  You’re quite fortunate your family member is willing to engage in mental health services. Just because these interventions haven’t addressed her outlook to a point that relieves the pressure on you and your sibling doesn’t mean they can’t. You could ask your mother’s permission have a two-way conversation with the counselor to work on some topics to her, e.g. “Mom, since I’m far away and can’t always talk, can I ask your counselor to follow up on a few things I might not have time to get to?” If she won’t go for that, you can email or leave voicemails to the counselor and psychiatrist. They may not be getting the full picture from her. Seems prudent to at least try with the trained, human professionals who know her before resorting to AI. As others suggested you could also seek different providers but only if Mom likes that idea.

It's a lot safer to decide to change your diet a little bit to increase say, your intake of B12 or zinc from food instead of popping pills. You should resort to pills only if you cannot or will not change your diet to a healthy omnivorous diet that covers everything.

comments.body: Can we just for once put politics aside and admit that a drop of homeless population is good news? If whatever policy that was started or has been ongoing is working, then that's the path we can keep pushing forward. I don't really care if it's Trump or Dems who take credit for it, so long as we see the positive outcome, that's what I care about.

comments.name: Susan Joy
comments.body: There are fewer than a million homeless? Hard to believe so few are degrading the quality of life for so many. I’d be happy to pay to build a commune in the middle of the desert or mountains, drop in supplies periodically, have it far enough away that it would be very hard for them to travel back to set up their tents in public parks. Provide satellite so those who wish can have amusements or search for jobs or find housing in population centers. Drug addicts will be forced to make do and the mentally ill will have shelter and food. Shall we start a go fund me? I’m sure we’ll get millions to contribute hundreds of millions to have somewhere to send those who will not accept help or social services but would rather commandeer our public parks and sidewalks.

comments.name: Laurel
comments.body: What about deaths as a reducer of the homeless population?  Life on the streets is dangerous for both health and crime reasons. Many, many homeless are older, or been forced onto the streets by medical bankruptcy or have bad health from yars of addiction.

comments.name: Benjamin
comments.body: Well, that's some good news.  I used to volunteer pretty often at a homeless shelter and I observed the conditions of the people outside the shelters.  I thought the proposed changes to dealing with homelessness by the Trump administration were counter productive.  People really need to be off the streets with a roof over their heads and whatever support they need.  The proposed change of forcing people into mental health treatment and then releasing them to the streets guarantees they will be back.

comments.name: Vulgarity

Violations of fundamental humanity and autonomy, the implementation of those violations, is vulgar. 

I am truly sorry for the human beings who, in the act of violating fundamental humanity and autonomy, are so used to playing ridiculous surface variable manipulation games, that they are blind to the vulgarity of their acts and instead interpret that word to mean something literal and juvenile. 

However, thank you for proving my overall point. Methodologies that refuse to be restrained by humanity and human autonomy are flawed at their core - in addition to being immoral and against fundamental principles, they inevitably lead to incompetence and are therefore counterproductive to their intended (as presented) goals - because all they reflect is their own perspective.

He said they put ‘rat poison’ in cigarettes, but that was Wigand the Scientist not knowing the difference between the   traditional flavorant coumarin and the blood thinner/rat poison coumadin. When that lie was rebutted, he switched to a new lie that ‘toilet bowl cleaner’ was put in commercial cigarettes. A gullible media hungry for heroes bought his baloney, and when the old cigarette company committed an ‘own goal’ of trying to besmirch his character, Wigand was forever deified by the WSJ and the broader media. Almost everything he says is a falsehood, as anyone who studied up on this character knows.

comments.body: I and nearly everyone I know are well over fifty, and if we want something, we buy it for ourselves. We see no reason to clutter other people's dwellings with objects our consumer culture commands us to purchase. If I give anything other than my best wishes to anyone, it's a book with the stipulation that if they don't like it after a few pages they are to stop reading it and pass it on to someone who might.

I also have no problem asking my adult kids for gift suggestions, that way they are assured of getting what they want with no money wasted.

comments.name: Moritz
comments.body:
I wonder why these supermarket fridges were remote controllable in the first place?

Maybe one lesson to be learned here is that connecting stuff to the internet is not always a good idea. Making stuff remote controllable when there’s little to no reason for it is just asking for trouble. 

And the bigger lessons we have to learn is that (1) there are indeed bad actors out there, and we have to build our systems accordingly; and (2) redundancies and frictions are not always just inefficiencies to be removed, but often the things that stand between us and total chaos when stuff goes wrong (which happens all the time, and even more so if you have bad actors out there).

comments.body:
Each time Pareles posts a list, I listen to it, hoping to find something I like, and each time go away empty-handed. 

I recently learned that when Pareles reviewed Mariah Carey's now-classic Christmas album, he accused the young woman of "turning expressions of devotion into narcissistic displays." In truth, she made those songs her own in a good way. They are some of the best renditions of those songs available. And this approach is itself a way of expressing reverence. In any case, if he missed the boat with this album, maybe I shouldn't be surprised that he doesn't reveal the songs that are going to be future gems.

(Granted, this is all very subjective.)

comments.name: Elizabeth B
comments.body:
As any property owner knows, a rushed construction job is always a mistake. Especially in the case of Trump’s self-aggrandizing projects, failure to consult with environmental, historical, cultural, and landmark groups will only lead to ugly, grandiose, and faulty megaliths that most Americans do not want in their capital.

It should also be noted that most of these projects (the ballroom, the elite golf course taking over a public park and golf course, fencing in Lafayette Square Park, gold all over the White House, etc., etc.) will be restricted to only the wealthy and political insiders. Most Washingtonians and Americans will have no access to them. 

Ironic, since we, the American taxpayers, are the people paying for these projects — despite Trump’s claim that he’s paying out of his own pocket (the ballroom) or that MAGA donors are paying for them.

Trump should restrict his dreams of grandeur to tarting up Mira Lago. Or maybe he should build a new casino.

comments.name: Betsy Smith
comments.body: The President is the temporary occupant of the White House.  He does not own it or the surrounding property, the District of Columbia.  They belong to "We, the People."  He needs to undo the damage he has done so far, do the necessary repairs (e.g., tear down the "ballroom/fortress"and replace the East Wing as it was, brick by brick) and to refrain from any future construction projects.  He can do whatever he likes at Mar-a-Lago, since that is his house.  The White house is mine, and yours, and ours.
